power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 1", Sentence = "To examine the consequences of the construction of the intervals when these differences are comparable to the standard errors, we consider the location-shift model where p = 1, b l ∈ R and c > 0 are constants, σ > 0 is known, and ˆ︁ Σ = σ 2 ."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 164 columns across 26 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 26 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 7 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:7, File = c("01_sources_data.R", "02_estimation_temperature_mortality.R", 
"isimip3.R", "03_climate_change_scenarios.R", "04_demographic_scenarios.R", 
"05_aggregation_impacts.R", "06_plots.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"01_sources_data.R", "—", "01_sources_data.R, 02_estimation_temperature_mortality.R, isimip3.R", 
"01_sources_data.R", "01_sources_data.R", "01_sources_data.R, 02_estimation_temperature_mortality.R"
), Basis = c("numeric", "dependency", "numeric", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, 
-7L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**6 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/gasparrini/2019_vicedo-cabrera_Epidem_Rcodedata/refs/heads/master/lndn_obs.csv` to `indata/raw/lndn_obs.csv` (in 01_sources_data.R); `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IPCC-WG1/Atlas/main/warming-levels/CMIP6_Atlas_WarmingLevels.csv` to `indata/raw/CMIP6_Atlas_WarmingLevels.csv` (in 01_sources_data.R); `data_proj_temp_biascorrection_ssp245.RData` to `outdata/file/02_calibrated_climate_projections/data_proj_temp_biascorrection_ssp245.RData` (in 06_plots.R); `correction_factor_spatialcal_ssp2.RData` to `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/correction_factor_spatialcal_ssp2.RData` (in 06_plots.R); `data_proj_mort_spatialcal_ssp2.RData` to `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/data_proj_mort_spatialcal_ssp2.RData` (in 06_plots.R); `data_proj_mort_spatialcal_tempcal_ssp2.RData` to `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/data_proj_mort_spatialcal_tempcal_ssp2.RData` (in 06_plots.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Files not run on their own
1 file only defines functions, so running it on its own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

```{r}

-1L), class = "data.frame")

```
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 6 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **A script looked for 4 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running it once more we copied them there: `outdata/file/02_calibrated_climate_projections/data_proj_temp_biascorrection_ssp245.RData` to `outdata/file/02_calibrated_climate_projections/outdata/file/02_calibrated_climate_projections/data_proj_temp_biascorrection_ssp245.RData` for `06_plots.R`; `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/correction_factor_spatialcal_ssp2.RData` to `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/correction_factor_spatialcal_ssp2.RData` for `06_plots.R`; `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/data_proj_mort_spatialcal_ssp2.RData` to `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/data_proj_mort_spatialcal_ssp2.RData` for `06_plots.R`; `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/data_proj_mort_spatialcal_tempcal_ssp2.RData` to `outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/outdata/file/03_calibrated_demographic_projections/data_proj_mort_spatialcal_tempcal_ssp2.RData` for `06_plots.R`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

info.title: Coverage of Empirical Confidence Intervals for the Ensemble Mean of General Circulation Models in Projecting Climate Change Impacts on Health

text.text: In projections of climate change impacts on health, the mean impact across general circulation models (GCMs) is commonly reported with an empirical confidence interval (eCI) formed from quantiles of impacts pooled across GCMs and coefficient draws.
We specify the estimands and predictands and examine intervals aligned with them.
The eCI is aligned with the impact under a GCM selected uniformly at random from the considered set, and its nominal level does not indicate its coverage for the mean.
We examine coverage as the observed-data sample size increases, with a fixed number of GCMs and infinitely many coefficient draws.
At the 95% nominal level, coverage for the mean over the considered GCMs converges to one with fewer than 40 GCMs unless their impacts are all equal, and can converge to zero with more than 40.
When GCMs are sampled independently from a population with a normal distribution of impacts, coverage for the population mean converges to 0.75 and 0.9375 for three and five GCMs, respectively.
For each of the two estimands and two predictands, we identify an interval whose coverage converges to the nominal level under the respective assumptions.
In simulated heat-related mortality projections, coverage of the 95% eCI for the mean over the considered GCMs was at least 0.99 in 22 of 26 settings.
A London reanalysis illustrates the differences between the intervals.

Future health impacts of climate change are commonly projected by combining an exposureresponse function estimated from observed data with future exposure trajectories generated by multiple general circulation models (GCMs).
text.formatted: Future health impacts of climate change are commonly projected by combining an exposureresponse function estimated from observed data with future exposure trajectories generated by multiple general circulation models <ref type="bibr">(GCMs)</ref>.

text.text: For each GCM, the impact of interest, such as the number of heat-related deaths in a future period, is projected by applying the estimated exposure-response function to the exposure trajectory of the GCM, and the GCM-specific impacts are aggregated into their arithmetic mean, which we refer to as the GCM-ensemble mean.

The estimation uncertainty of the exposure-response function is propagated by drawing coefficients from an approximate sampling distribution of the estimator and computing the impact under each GCM with each draw.

The empirical confidence interval (eCI) is then defined as the interval between the empirical quantiles of the impacts pooled across the GCMs and the coefficient draws (Vicedo-Cabrera et al., 2019; Quijal-Zamorano et al., 2026), and it is reported together with the GCM-ensemble mean.
text.formatted: The empirical confidence interval (eCI) is then defined as the interval between the empirical quantiles of the impacts pooled across the GCMs and the coefficient draws <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Vicedo-Cabrera et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Quijal-Zamorano et al., 2026)</ref>, and it is reported together with the GCM-ensemble mean.

text.text: This procedure has been used in multicountry projections of temperature-and heatwave-related mortality and in projections of temperature-related cardiovascular hospitalizations (Gasparrini et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2021; Zhan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This procedure has been used in multicountry projections of temperature-and heatwave-related mortality and in projections of temperature-related cardiovascular hospitalizations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Gasparrini et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Guo et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Yang et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Zhan et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Chen et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the eCI, both the variation among the GCMs and the estimation uncertainty of the exposure-response function are summarized.
However, the eCI is constructed from the quantiles of the impacts pooled across the GCMs, whereas the reported point estimate is their mean.
Therefore, the nominal level of the eCI does not imply the same coverage probability for the GCM-ensemble mean, and it is not clear which quantity the eCI covers with the nominal probability.

The variation among the GCMs also raises the question of whether the target of the inference is the mean over the GCMs considered in the study or the mean over a population of GCMs from which the GCMs considered in the study are regarded as a sample.
This is because the multi-model ensembles in climate science are not designed as a random sample of models (Tebaldi and Knutti, 2007; Knutti et al., 2013; Abramowitz et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This is because the multi-model ensembles in climate science are not designed as a random sample of models <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Tebaldi and Knutti, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Knutti et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Abramowitz et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In this study, we specify the targets for which the GCM-ensemble mean is reported and the intervals aligned with each of them, and we evaluate the coverage of the eCI for these targets.

We consider four targets: two estimands (the mean impact over the considered GCMs and the mean impact over a population of GCMs) and two predictands (the impact under a GCM selected uniformly at random from the considered set and the impact under a new GCM).

In terms of these targets, we clarify that the eCI used in previous studies is an interval aligned with the first predictand, and we show that its coverage for the two estimands can deviate from the nominal level.
We then examine the intervals in a simulation study mimicking projections of heat-related mortality and in a reanalysis of the projections in London in the tutorial of Quijal-Zamorano et al. (2026).
text.formatted: We then examine the intervals in a simulation study mimicking projections of heat-related mortality and in a reanalysis of the projections in London in the tutorial of <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Quijal-Zamorano et al. (2026)</ref>.

Note that, since I µ (α) is computed from the same coefficient draws as the eCI, it can be obtained in existing projections without additional computation.
The targets can also be related to the impact under the actual climate, depending on how the GCMs are related to the actual climate.
Annan and Hargreaves (2010) contrasted two paradigms for interpreting multi-model ensembles in climate science.
In the truth-centred paradigm, the GCMs are regarded as sampled from a distribution centered on the actual climate.
If this centering also holds for the impacts, the impact under the actual climate corresponds to µ ∞ (θ 0 ).
In the paradigm of a statistically indistinguishable ensemble, the actual climate is regarded as exchangeable with the GCMs.
If the GCMs and the actual climate are regarded as independent draws from the same population, the impact under the actual climate corresponds to H new (θ 0 ).
If the actual climate is regarded as one of the considered GCMs, each with the probability 1/L, the impact under the actual climate corresponds to H s (θ 0 ).

In practice, however, the GCMs in multi-model ensembles share components and code, and some GCMs are near-replicates of others (Knutti et al., 2013; Abramowitz et al., 2019), so that the effective number of independent GCMs may be smaller than L, and the population of GCMs over which µ ∞ (θ 0 ) is defined may not be specified in practice (Tebaldi and Knutti, 2007).

This study has the following limitations.

With a small number of coefficient draws, the endpoints of the intervals are subject to Monte Carlo error, which was small relative to the differences between the intervals for the total population in the reanalysis with J = 100.

The coverage of I µ (α) for µ L (θ 0 ) relies on the consistency of n ˆ︁ Σ for Σ 0 in Assumption 1, which may not hold for the estimator in Section 4.2 if the conditional variance of the daily number of deaths given the covariates is not proportional to the conditional mean.
In such cases, a sandwich estimator can be used for ˆ︁ Σ without changing the construction of the intervals.
The intervals for µ ∞ (θ 0 ) assume that the GCMs are sampled independently from a population.
We did not consider other sources of uncertainty, such as the bias correction of the GCM outputs, the internal variability of the climate, and the demographic scenarios.

The coefficient vector θ 0 was computed by least squares on 1,000 equally spaced temperatures between the boundary knots.

The knots of the natural cubic spline basis were the percentiles of a temperature series of 500 years generated in the same manner as the observed temperature, and they were -1.38, 4.55, 15.75, 18.41, and 24.34.
The basis was computed for the scaled temperature (T -15)/10, and it is linear below the lower boundary knot and above the upper boundary knot.
In the computation of H l (θ), we rounded the temperature down to bins of width 0.1 • C and evaluated f θ at the midpoints of the bins, and H l (θ 0 ) was computed in the same manner.
In the large-ensemble design, the L -1 members with ∆ l = 2.5 had temperature series generated independently, so that the members differ only in the internal variability.
